questions.solution:
$\displaystyle\int x^{n}\,dx = \mathbf{\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C}$.

The condition $n \neq -1$ matters: at $n = -1$ the formula would divide by zero, and indeed $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C$ instead — a logarithm, not a power.

questions.q: The fundamental theorem of calculus states that $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ equals:
questions.solution:
$\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \mathbf{F(b) - F(a)}$, where $F$ is any antiderivative of $f$.

The theorem is remarkable because it links two things with no obvious connection: **area under a curve** and **antidifferentiation**. Note that any antiderivative will do, since the constants cancel in the subtraction.

questions.q: If $f$ is an **odd** function, then $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx$ equals:
questions.solution:
An odd function satisfies $f(-x) = -f(x)$, so its graph has rotational symmetry about the origin.

The signed area from $-a$ to $0$ exactly cancels the area from $0$ to $a$, giving $\mathbf{0}$.

For an **even** function the two halves are equal instead, so $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f = 2\int_0^a f$. Spotting the symmetry first often removes the need to integrate at all.

questions.q: The order of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3} = 0$ is:
questions.solution:
The **order** is the order of the **highest derivative** present, which here is the second derivative. So the order is $\mathbf{2}$.

The **degree** is the power of that highest derivative once the equation is polynomial in derivatives — here the second derivative appears to the first power, so the degree is 1.

The cube on $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ affects neither, since it is not the highest derivative.

$\displaystyle\int e^{x}\,dx = \mathbf{e^{x} + C}$.

$e^{x}$ is the unique function (up to a constant multiple) that is its own derivative, and so also its own integral. That property is what makes it central to the solution of differential equations.

questions.q: The integrating factor for $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where $P$ and $Q$ are functions of $x$, is:
questions.solution:
The integrating factor is $\text{IF} = \mathbf{e^{\int P\,dx}}$.

Multiplying through by it makes the left side an exact derivative, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(y\cdot\text{IF})$, so the equation integrates directly:

$y \cdot \text{IF} = \displaystyle\int Q \cdot \text{IF}\,dx + C$

Note it depends on $P$ alone, never on $Q$.

options: Reversing the limits reverses the sign
questions.solution:
**Reversing the limits of integration reverses the sign.** It follows immediately from the fundamental theorem:

$\displaystyle\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$ and $\displaystyle\int_b^a f = F(a) - F(b)$, which are negatives of each other.

A corollary is that $\displaystyle\int_a^a f(x)\,dx = 0$ always, whatever $f$ is.

questions.q: The area bounded by $y = f(x)$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = a$, $x = b$ (with $f \ge 0$) is:
questions.solution:
The area is $\mathbf{\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx}$, provided $f(x) \ge 0$ throughout.

Where $f$ dips below the axis the integral counts that region as **negative**, so for a genuine geometric area the curve must be split at its roots and the absolute values added:

$\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_a^b |f(x)|\,dx$

Forgetting this is the most common error in area problems.

questions.q: The general solution of a differential equation of order $n$ contains:
questions.solution:
A differential equation of order $n$ has a general solution with exactly $\mathbf{n}$ arbitrary constants — one for each integration performed.

Fixing those constants requires $n$ initial or boundary conditions, and the result is a **particular** solution.

This is why a second-order equation of motion needs both an initial position and an initial velocity.

$\displaystyle\int_0^2 x\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{4}{2} - 0 = \mathbf{2}$.

Geometrically this is the area of a triangle with base 2 and height 2, which is $\tfrac12(2)(2) = 2$ ✓

$x^{5}$ is an **odd** function, since $(-x)^{5} = -x^{5}$, and the limits are symmetric about the origin.

So the integral is $\mathbf{0}$ without any calculation.

Checking the long way: $\left[\dfrac{x^{6}}{6}\right]_{-3}^{3} = \dfrac{729}{6} - \dfrac{729}{6} = 0$ ✓

questions.q: What is the degree of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{3} + \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$?
questions.solution:
The highest derivative is $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$, so the **order** is 2.

The **degree** is the power to which that highest derivative is raised, which is $\mathbf{3}$.

Degree is only defined when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives, so an equation containing $\sin\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)$ has no degree.

questions.q: Find the area, in square units, bounded by $y = x^{2}$, the $x$-axis, $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.
questions.solution:
$\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_0^3 x^{2}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_0^3$

$= \dfrac{27}{3} - 0 = \mathbf{9}$ square units.

$x^{2} \ge 0$ throughout the interval, so no splitting is needed.

questions.q: Explain the method of separation of variables and the integrating factor method for first-order differential equations. Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = 6$ with $y(0) = 0$, and interpret the behaviour of the solution as $x \to \infty$.
questions.solution:
**Method 1: separation of variables.**

Applies when the equation can be written as

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = g(x)h(y)$

so that all the $y$ terms can be gathered on one side and all the $x$ terms on the other:

$\dfrac{dy}{h(y)} = g(x)\,dx$

Integrating both sides gives the general solution, with one arbitrary constant. It is the simplest method and should always be tried first.

**Method 2: the integrating factor.**

Applies to any **linear** first-order equation, that is one of the form

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$

Even when the variables will not separate. The idea is to multiply through by a cleverly chosen function that turns the left side into an exact derivative.

Let $\text{IF} = e^{\int P\,dx}$. Multiplying through:

$\text{IF}\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P\cdot\text{IF}\cdot y = Q\cdot\text{IF}$

Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\text{IF}) = P\cdot\text{IF}$, the left side is exactly the product-rule expansion of $\dfrac{d}{dx}(y\cdot\text{IF})$. So

$\dfrac{d}{dx}(y\cdot\text{IF}) = Q\cdot\text{IF}$

and integrating:

$y\cdot\text{IF} = \displaystyle\int Q\cdot\text{IF}\,dx + C$

**Solving the given equation.**

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = 6$, with $y(0) = 0$.

This is linear with $P = 2$ and $Q = 6$.

$\int P\,dx = \int 2\,dx = 2x$, so $\text{IF} = e^{2x}$.

Multiply through:

$e^{2x}\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2e^{2x}y = 6e^{2x}$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{2x}\right) = 6e^{2x}$

Integrate both sides:

$ye^{2x} = \displaystyle\int 6e^{2x}\,dx = 3e^{2x} + C$

Divide by $e^{2x}$:

$y = 3 + Ce^{-2x}$

**Applying the initial condition.** At $x = 0$, $y = 0$:

$0 = 3 + C \Rightarrow C = -3$

$\boxed{y = 3\left(1 - e^{-2x}\right)}$

**Check.** $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6e^{-2x}$, and $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = 6e^{-2x} + 6 - 6e^{-2x} = 6$ ✓, with $y(0) = 3(1-1) = 0$ ✓

**Behaviour as $x \to \infty$.**

As $x$ grows, $e^{-2x} \to 0$, so

$y \to 3$

The solution **rises from 0 and approaches 3 asymptotically**, never quite reaching it. It is monotonically increasing, since $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6e^{-2x} > 0$ always, and its rate of increase decays exponentially.

**Why 3, and why this shape.** The solution has two parts. The constant $3$ is the **steady state**: setting $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ in the original equation gives $2y = 6$, so $y = 3$ is the value at which the system stops changing. The term $-3e^{-2x}$ is the **transient**, the part that remembers the initial condition and dies away.

This structure — a steady state plus a decaying transient — is the general shape of every stable linear first-order system, and the coefficient 2 sets how fast the transient dies. The same equation with the same solution describes a capacitor charging through a resistor, a body warming towards its surroundings by Newton's law of cooling, and a population approaching a carrying capacity under constant immigration.
